title: A comparison of two techniques used to seal root canals
official: Comparison of apical plugs versus single-cone obturation technique in root canal treatment. A randomised controlled trial
summary:
Background and study aims
Apical periodontitis is an infection around the tip of a tooth root. It is usually treated using root canal treatment, which removes infected tissue from inside the tooth and seals the root canal to prevent further infection. Root canal treatment is often completed over two visits.

There are different ways to seal the root canal after it has been cleaned. One common method uses a single gutta-percha cone together with a hydraulic calcium silicate cement sealer. Another method uses an apical plug made from hydraulic cement at the end of the root canal before the rest of the canal is filled. Apical plugs are commonly used in teeth with incomplete root formation and have shown good success rates. However, it is not clear whether this technique provides better healing outcomes than the standard single-cone method in teeth affected by apical periodontitis. This study aims to compare the effectiveness of an apical plug with a single-cone obturation technique in root canal treatment. The researchers will assess which method is more effective at promoting healing of apical periodontitis.

Who can participate?
Adults aged 18 to 80 years who have a permanent tooth diagnosed with apical periodontitis and require root canal treatment.

What does the study involve?
Participants will receive root canal treatment over two visits. Before treatment, participants will provide consent and may have dental radiographs or a cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) scan if needed. During the second visit, participants will be randomly allocated to one of two treatment groups. One group will receive an apical plug made from hydraulic cement, while the other group will receive a single-cone root canal filling with hydraulic cement sealer. Following treatment, participants will attend follow-up appointments at 6 and 12 months, where radiographs will be taken to assess healing.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Participants may not receive a direct benefit from taking part, but the findings could help improve root canal treatment for future patients. The treatments used in the study are established dental procedures that participants require as part of their routine dental care. As with any root canal treatment, there may be temporary discomfort or pain after treatment, and researchers will collect information about pain and any adverse events during the study.

Where is the study run from?
 The study is coordinated by the University of Birmingham and will take place in three private dental practices in England.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
September 2026 to September 2029.

Who is funding the study?
The study is investigator-initiated and funded.

Who is the main contact?
Prof Josette Camilleri, University of Birmingham, J.Camilleri@bham.ac.uk.

interventions.name:
Two-visit root canal treatment. The randomisation is through a computer-generated seed. 
Visit 1:
-	Consent and patient information sheet
-	Periapical radiograph and CBCT if necessary
-	Local anaesthesia and isolation
-	Access and Canal preparation as necessary

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1.	Permanent teeth diagnosed with apical periodontitis
2.	Apical diameter between 40 and 70
3.	Teeth suitable for root canal treatment
Exclusion criteria:
1.	Teeth with previous root canal treatment
2.	Teeth with curvatures >30 degrees
3.	Teeth with root fractures
4.	Teeth with incomplete root formation
5.	Patients with systemic diseases affecting bone metabolism
6.	Patients with inadequate oral hygiene with Plaque Index >20%
7.	Teeth that served as abutment for a fixed partial denture
8.	Teeth with periodontal probing depth≥ 6 mm
